results.title: How to Evaluate CPU Performance with Microbenchmarks
results.content: # How can microbenchmarks help you evaluate CPU performance? If you want to optimize your code for speed and efficiency, you need to measure how your CPU performs under different workloads and scenarios. Microbenchmarks are small and focused tests that isolate specific aspects of CPU performance, such as arithmetic operations, memory access, cache behavior, or instruction pipelining. In this article, you will learn how to use microbenchmarks to evaluate CPU performance and identify potential bottlenecks and improvements in your code. ## 1 What are microbenchmarks? Microbenchmarks are short and simple programs that measure the execution time or throughput of a specific CPU operation or feature. For example, a microbenchmark can test how fast your CPU can add two integers, or how much latency it incurs when accessing a memory location. Microbenchmarks are useful for comparing different CPUs, compilers, or optimization techniques, as well as for understanding the low-level behavior and characteristics of your CPU. Microbenchmarks focus on testing a single aspect of CPU performance, such as arithmetic operations, memory access, cache behavior, or instruction pipelining. This makes it easier to pinpoint bottlenecks and areas for improvement.By running the same microbenchmark on different CPUs, compilers, or with different optimization techniques, you can see how they compare in terms of performance. While not replicating real-world scenarios entirely, microbenchmarks offer predictive insights into CPU performance under specific workloads. Additionally, power-saving and frequency-scaling features should be disabled or minimized, and the CPU and cache should be warmed up before running the microbenchmark. Microbenchmarks are powerful and useful tools for evaluating CPU performance, but they should not be used as a replacement for a comprehensive and realistic performance analysis. To use microbenchmarks effectively and appropriately, you can identify CPU performance bottlenecks or hotspots in your code, compare different CPU performance optimization techniques, understand and optimize the CPU performance of specific algorithms or data structures, and learn about the CPU architecture. Microbenchmarks can help you measure the impact of optimization techniques, explore the features of the CPU architecture, and gain valuable insights into your code's performance. results.title: Microbenchmarks Considered Useful | Frappe Blog
results.content: I saw that Prime clip while I was working on microbenchmarks that measured small Python operations in microseconds or even nanoseconds. Microbenchmarks are small snippets of code, often just 2-10 lines that are run in a loop many times to get precise timing information. 4. If your language has Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation like JavaScript and recent versions of Python then the performance depends on how often a particular piece of code has run. So my plan was to do 100x small 1.01x changes that add up to a big number and microbenchmarks are a *perfect* tool for this problem. It's hard to isolate what change caused a 1% difference in overall performance but it's easy to spot a microbenchmark that showed a slowdown by 1.5x. So while the microbenchmark numbers don't mean anything on their own, tracking changes to that number over time help maintain software performance. Use whatever works for you, just don't try to fool someone into believing that microbenchmark numbers on their own mean something or worse...

results.title: Behavior of Colloidal Nanosilica in an Ultrahigh Performance Concrete Environment Using Dynamic Light Scattering
results.content: It was found that the sodium stabilized 20 nm NS sol remains dispersed at a solid concentration of 2 wt % through a variety of pH values with the inclusion of potassium ions. In previous research, parameters of interest included the type of NS, the size of the particles or the surface area, the concentration of NS, addition or replacement of cement, and water to cement ratios [11,12,13,14,15,16,17]. System I is a well-dispersed cementitious system with cement and microsized silica, representative of ultrahigh-performance concrete, exhibiting a high particle-packing density and thus enhanced mechanical and durability properties in comparison to conventional concrete [18]. NS particles are susceptible to form large agglomerates due to their very high specific surface area (50–750 m2/g). Therefore, adding well-dispersed NS to the concrete mixture can lead to agglomeration and gelation resulting from the release of ions during cement hydration. Silica can also be stabilized at low pH by removing all ions, resulting in slightly negatively charged particles, as this is the case with NS-20a used in this study. The parameters for testing the four NS sols from Table 1 included varying solid concentration by adding deionized (DI) water, varying pH value by adding 0.1 M aqueous potassium hydroxide (KOH) or 0.1 M hydrochloric acid (HCl), varying amounts of calcium nitrate (Ca(NO3)2·4H2O), and adding UHPC-like synthetic pore solution (PS) as outlined by Schrofl et al. All four NS sols were altered and measured for particle size distribution (PSD) and zeta potential (ZP). The effect of the concentration of NS particles was first studied to isolate the potential influence of the number of particles in a sol. Since this pore solution only contains water, KOH, and Ca(NO3)2 it can be inferred that the Ca(NO3)2 is the main contributor to NS agglomeration, due to its bridging effect between silica particles. **Figure 7.** ZP and size measurements for NS-20b: (**a**) solid concentration varied with DI water; (**b**) potassium hydroxide concentration varied with DI water; (**c**) calcium nitrate concentration varied with DI water; (**d**) pore solution concentration varied with DI water. **Figure 7.** ZP and size measurements for NS-20b: (**a**) solid concentration varied with DI water; (**b**) potassium hydroxide concentration varied with DI water; (**c**) calcium nitrate concentration varied with DI water; (**d**) pore solution concentration varied with DI water.
